extraction.name: RoboBench
extraction.description: A benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models as embodied brains for robotic manipulation across five dimensions, 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs.
extraction.creator: Yulin Luo, Chun-Kai Fan, Menghang Dong, Jiayu Shi, Mengdi Zhao, Bo-Wen Zhang, Cheng Chi, Jiaming Liu, Gaole Dai, Rongyu Zhang, Ruichuan An, Kun Wu, Zhengping Che, Shaoxuan Xie, Guocai Yao, Zhongxia Zhao, Pengwei Wang, Guang Liu, Zhongyuan Wang, Tiejun Huang, Shanghang Zhang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was built from open-source and in-house robotic data, with dimension-specific construction workflows and annotations from MLLMs, detection models, human annotators, and experts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Open-source and in-house robotic data, including large-scale real-world robotic datasets and high-quality robotic videos.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The authors extracted frame sequences as standardized inputs, standardized data into multiple-choice QA, applied general and task-specific filters during construction, and removed or manually reviewed items after validation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were produced using LLMs/MLLMs and humans depending on the subtask: implicit instructions were rewritten using LLMs; perception used GPT-generated functional properties, Gemini-segmented video steps, manual annotations of positions and keypoint changes, and human-labeled bounding boxes; planning used Gemini-generated structured annotations refined by human annotators; affordance frames were annotated with static, dynamic, and mobile affordances; failure analysis used expert labels and synthetic perturbations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The benchmark used post-construction validation by 20 professionally trained annotators and a majority-vote strategy; items all models solved correctly were removed, and items all models failed were manually reviewed and corrected.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: LLMs, GPT, Gemini, MLLMs, detection models
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that planning-level failures were synthesized because real-world planning failure data were lacking, and that existing planning data primarily focus on concrete action execution without explicitly distinguishing left-right arm assignments or positional movements.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark has limited real-world planning failure data, so planning-level failures are synthesized; human performance on execution-level failure diagnosis is also relatively low, indicating intrinsic task difficulty.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating MLLMs as embodied brains for robotic manipulation across instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis.

name.evidence: To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboBench, a benchmark that systematically evaluates multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as embodied brains.

description.evidence: Motivated by the critical roles across the full manipulation pipeline, RoboBench defines five dimensions—instruction comprehension, perception reasoning, generalized planning, affordance prediction, and failure analysis—spanning 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To evaluate the five cognitive dimensions, we build datasets from open-source and in-house robotic data, enriched with MLLM- and human-provided annotations, aligning each sub-benchmark with the embodied task pipeline for realism.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: To evaluate the five cognitive dimensions, we build datasets from open-source and in-house robotic data, enriched with MLLM- and human-provided annotations, aligning each sub-benchmark with the embodied task pipeline for realism.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Data combine large-scale real-world robotic datasets Fang et al. (2023); Collaboration et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024c); Wu et al. (2024); Bu et al. (2025) with curated in-house collection, narrowing the sim-to-real gap.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We build a planning pool from high-quality robotic videos Collaboration et al. (2023); Lin et al. (2024a); Liu et al. (2024b;c); Fang et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2024); Mu et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2024), extracting frame sequences as standardized inputs. All data are standardized into multiple-choice QA. We apply both general and task-specific filters. General criteria address image quality and task validity, while sub-benchmarks have tailored rules—such as excluding single-arm data from dual-arm tasks.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Explicit instructions are drawn from daily-life scenarios with clearly specified actions and targets, whereas implicit instructions are obtained by rewriting them into demand-based requests using LLMs. Perception Reasoning: Accurate perception is essential for reliable planning and execution. We construct datasets across four aspects: robotic-centric, using real robot data with type and view metadata for template-based QA; object-centric, combining curated static attributes Gao et al. (2024) with GPT-generated functional properties and distractors; scene-centric, leveraging Gemini-segmented video steps for temporal grounding, together with manual annotations of relative positions and keypoint changes for spatial and causal reasoning; and task-centric, with human-labeled bounding boxes linking long-horizon instructions to target objects. Gemini Comanici et al. (2025) generates structured annotations—task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, and metadata (objects, actions, scenes, embodiments)—which are refined by human annotators. From the planning pool, representative frames are sampled and annotated with three types of affordance: static (contact points), dynamic (motion trajectories), and mobile (base positions). Execution-level failures (e.g., position misalignment, trajectory deviations, gripper errors) are collected from RoboMIND Wu et al. (2024) and labeled by experts, while planning-level failures are synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order) due to lack of real-world planning failure data.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: After data construction, we recruite 20 professionally trained annotators to conduct comprehensive quality inspections, validating linguistic clarity, answerability, and correctness Liu et al. (2024d). We further adopt a majority-vote strategy Liu et al. (2024d): items that all models solve correctly are removed, whereas items all models fail to solve undergo manual review and correction.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: Explicit instructions are drawn from daily-life scenarios with clearly specified actions and targets, whereas implicit instructions are obtained by rewriting them into demand-based requests using LLMs. object-centric, combining curated static attributes Gao et al. (2024) with GPT-generated functional properties and distractors; scene-centric, leveraging Gemini-segmented video steps for temporal grounding. Gemini Comanici et al. (2025) generates structured annotations—task summaries, step-wise instructions with timestamps, and metadata (objects, actions, scenes, embodiments)—which are refined by human annotators. Each workflow generally follows three stages—preprocessing, annotation with VLMs, detection models or human experts, and Q&A format generation.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Execution-level failures (e.g., position misalignment, trajectory deviations, gripper errors) are collected from RoboMIND Wu et al. (2024) and labeled by experts, while planning-level failures are synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order) due to lack of real-world planning failure data. We attribute this to the nature of existing planning data, which primarily focuses on concrete action execution without explicitly distinguishing between left–right arm assignments or positional movements.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Execution-level failures (e.g., position misalignment, trajectory deviations, gripper errors) are collected from RoboMIND Wu et al. (2024) and labeled by experts, while planning-level failures are synthesized by perturbing correct instructions (wrong object, missing step, wrong order) due to lack of real-world planning failure data. Even human performance remains relatively low in such cases — 47.30 compared to 80.67 in planning error — highlighting the intrinsic difficulty of this task.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce RoboBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as embodied brains across 5 key dimensions, spanning 14 capabilities, 25 tasks, and 6092 QA pairs.
